author: Tharun Loknath
text:
I recently interviewed for 10+ AI Engineering roles, and the experience was both interesting and surprising.

One thing became very clear: only a handful of companies truly know how to interview AI engineers.

Some well-known companies were still running interviews as if it were 2021.

One company spent almost the entire system design round on API design, even though the role was focused on building agentic AI systems. There wasn’t a single discussion around MCP, agent orchestration, evaluation, or LLM architecture.

Another company focused heavily on database design for an AI Engineer role building agentic chatbots. Again, very little discussion around AI-specific design decisions.

A few companies are also sticking to traditional live coding with no AI tools allowed—even for senior AI Engineering roles. Strong coding fundamentals matter, but this feels disconnected from how modern AI software is actually built.

On the other hand, the AI-native companies were refreshing.

One interview had me build a tool using coding agents while explaining every decision—what I decided versus what the AI decided. That tells you whether someone actually understands these tools, their limitations, context management, and how to work with them effectively.

Another standout round focused entirely on evaluation frameworks: How do you measure an AI system? How do you know it’s improving? In my opinion, that’s one of the hardest parts of AI Engineering, and companies asking these questions usually know exactly what they’re hiring for.

Another trend I’ve noticed is that many AI Engineering roles are slowly becoming Software Engineering roles with LLMs.

Strong software engineering is essential, but it’s only half the job.

The other half is ML thinking: turning AI problems into optimization problems, defining the right evaluation metrics, monitoring quality, detecting drift, and knowing when a system is actually getting better.

Without solid evaluation and monitoring, you’re flying blind. As ML Engineers, we’re trained to think about how AI systems fail—and how to detect those failures before users do.

The best AI Engineers understand both software systems and machine learning systems.

My biggest takeaway? The market is still diluted.

A small number of companies with real ML/AI experience know exactly what they need. Many others want AI Engineers, but the interview process shows they haven’t yet figured out what skills actually matter.

If you’re interviewing, evaluate the company too.

Ask how they evaluate AI systems, what their production monitoring looks like, how they think about agentic systems, and what success looks like beyond writing code.

Their answers will tell you everything about the maturity of their AI organization.

Your AI/ML expertise is valuable. Your time is too. Make sure the company deserves both.
